title: Down River
subtitle: Minneapolis, Memphis and New Orleans
focus: The Minneapolis sound and the fight to own your own name, Memphis blues and sanctified guitar, and New Orleans second line, brass bands, funk drumming and bounce

intro.t: Here is what I know. Low's little book says Memphis, then New Orleans, then overseas. Down the river, every one of them.
So, logically, south. Memphis is south. New Orleans is extremely south. I have a map. It agrees with me.
Listen. You don't walk into a river in the middle. You start where it starts. Then you know what it carried.
Fun fact - the Mississippi starts at a lake in Minnesota so small you can walk across it on -
Tuesday. Not now. I'm being wise.
Besides, I got a cousin in Minneapolis. Plays keytar at weddings. Says the cold keeps him in tune.
The music came up this river with a cardboard suitcase. You are taking it back down in a church van.
Tuesday rides up front with the Evidence Box on her knees. Item one, item two, item three. She checks the latches at every toll booth.
Eleven hundred miles north so you can go south. Cross calls it scenic. The van calls it a hill.

outro.t: Sunday. Nine o'clock. The van parked on a levee road with the engine ticking, the phone on speaker on the dashboard, everybody leaning in.
She does not open with 'Who showed up?' She has opened with it every single Sunday since you left Harlem.
I heard myself on the radio this morning. Laughing. In between the weather and a mattress sale.
The label took my voice and never asked. You took my voice and never asked.
The difference is asking, baby. It was only ever asking.
I'll take it down. Nana, I'll take it down right now, I'll -
Can't take it down, baby. That's the trouble with a voice.
She hangs up first. She has never once hung up first, on anybody. Up front, Ruth has taken off her hat.
I didn't ask her. I knew she'd say no. That's... that's the whole thing, isn't it.

gigs.title: Five Blank Stars
gigs.blurb: A club with a wall of painted stars, and an owner who knows what a name costs.

challenge.text: Lake only paints the bright ones. Earn a gold star on one song.

before.t: Minneapolis in July. The outside wall of the club is painted black and covered in silver stars, and every star has a name in it.
Four hundred and twelve stars. I counted twice. The second time Uncle Cross made me stop at ninety and buy him a lemonade.
Everybody who was somebody played this room. Everybody who wasn't yet, too. That's the good part.
A man on a ladder is painting a new one. Small, quiet, silver to the elbow. He does not come down.
You're the van.
We're the band. The van's just louder about it.
Mm.
Excuse me, sir. Do you ever paint a star without a name in it?
No.
He paints two more points before he says anything else. Lake does not waste paint, and he does not waste words.
Man from this town gave up his own name once. Rather go without one than let a contract keep it.
People laughed. He didn't. He got it back.
Wish I'd had that kind of nerve in '86.
Names are expensive. That's why people take them. Go on in. I'll listen from up here.
Inside, the drum machine in the booth counts off at one-twelve. It has never been rushed by anybody. Neither has Lake.

afterWin.t: Two in the morning. The club is letting out, and Lake is already back up the ladder with a work light and a can of silver.
He paints five stars in a row, low on the wall, where anybody walking past could touch them. He leaves them empty.
You forgot the names.
Didn't forget.
Those are for them?
Come back with names.
For the record, I am photographing a wall at two in the morning. Five stars, unfilled. Photograph only. The wall stays in Minneapolis.
Nobody ever held a wall for me. Man holds a wall for you, you come back. That's manners.
Five empty stars on a black wall. Sixty years, and somebody finally drew my family portrait.

afterLose.t: Paint's still wet. Come back up.
The drum machine doesn't mind. It will count you in all night. Run it back.

gigs.title: Trade Fours
gigs.blurb: Saturday night on Beale. An 86-year-old in a church hat wants to hear what you've got, four bars at a time.

challenge.text: Trade fours with Saturday Ruth and don't blink: hit 400 notes in a row.

before.t: Saturday night on Beale. Neon, brass leaking out of three doors at once, and a juke so small the band and the bar share an outlet.
Low's book: 'Sister (Ruth) - Memphis, Beale, Saturdays.' That is the most specific clue we have ever had. It's practically an address.
Listen. You don't play one street every Saturday for sixty years unless you love it or you're hiding on it.
On the little stage, under a wide church hat with a silk flower on the brim, an old woman with a hollow-body guitar has a room full of grown men hollering like it's Sunday.
Excuse me, ma'am. Are you Sister Ruth?
Child, I'm nobody's sister on a Saturday. Sister is a Sunday word. Tonight I'm Ruth, and I'm working.
A church van, parked on Beale Street, on a Saturday night. Somebody upstairs has got jokes.
We came a long way to ask you something.
Everybody's asking. Nobody's playing. You want to ask me something, baby, ask me in fours.
Cutting contest. The old way. She plays four bars, you answer with four, back and forth till somebody runs dry.
Or till I get bored. I'm eighty-six. I get bored quick and I play slow. Don't you rush me.
Technically we haven't established that she's -
Technically, child, you're standing on my cord.
She tunes without looking, the way you lace a shoe. Four bars, and then she nods at you. Your turn.

afterWin.t: Somewhere around the ninth trade nobody in the juke can tell who is teaching who. Then Ruth stops playing and starts laughing, and it takes her a good while to stop.
Sixty years I been Saturday Ruth so the Sunday folks wouldn't know. The whole church knew by 1970. They just liked having something to pray about.
So you're Sister.
She unbuckles her strap. Tooled leather, worn through at the shoulder. Folded small inside the lining, soft as cloth, is a page torn out of a hymnal.
Item four. Page two-eleven, 'Watchman, Hold the Light.' Pencil in the margin: 'sing it C.F.'s way.' C.F. is Clementine Fontaine. That's Nana's mother.
Dess's mama tore it out and put it in my hand on the church steps. Then we went round the corner and put a backbeat under a prayer.
You keep the page, child. I'll keep the strap. It's still holding me up.
Somebody just plugged a guitar into me. I can feel the hum.
Wendell went home to the brass band in New Orleans, last I knew. Now. Which seat in that van is the front seat?
...That's my seat.
It was, baby.

afterLose.t: Not yet, baby. I'm eighty-six. I got time. Y'all got till Watch Night.
Come on back up here and trade with me again. I was just getting warm.

gigs.title: Second Line
gigs.blurb: Deacon's old brass band still marches here. Nobody has seen him since the flood.

vibe.label: New Orleans funk, brass and bounce

challenge.text: March it clean: 88% on every song, the way a second line keeps its feet.

before.t: New Orleans. Air you could wring out like a towel. A brass band comes down the street past the Blues House doors, tuba first, and half the sidewalk falls in behind it without deciding to.
Now that's a second line! Nobody asked those people to dance. They just went.
For the record, I can see it from the back seat. Barely. Around a box.
Ruth walks straight into the street in her church hat and stops the tuba player with one finger.
Baby, I'm looking for Wendell Arceneaux. Little man. Snare drum. Tapped on anything that held still.
The tuba player knows the name. After the water in 2005, a lot of this city went somewhere else to stay alive, and Wendell went too. Nobody on this block knows where.
Somebody knows. Somebody always knows. We just ain't met them yet.
Tuesday, alone in the back of the parked van. The Evidence Box for a desk. The reel's transfer open on her laptop. Everybody else asleep.
Pryce said keep the man under the hiss to ourselves. Fine. So I cut him out.
Roll call. The laugh. The count. Nothing before it. 'Do you know these voices?'
She does not wake anybody. She does not call Harlem. She knows exactly what Harlem would say. She posts it.
MORNING
The noon set at the Blues House. Tuesday has not slept. Her phone is face down on the table, buzzing like a hive.
Child, your pocket's ringing.
It's fine. It's nothing. It's probably nothing. Play. Play first.

afterWin.t: Halfway through your closer, last night's second line comes back around the corner and walks straight in the front door. Tuba first.
Nine million. Nine million plays since three in the morning. It's on every phone in this room. It's on the TUBA PLAYER'S phone.
Nine million? 'Lamppost Power' didn't do nine million in nine years.
Five voices from a back room in 1967, answering a roll call, all over the world before lunch. I have been famous before. I have never been introduced.
And there's a voice message. From Houston. From a church.
Good morning, baby, this is Mother Viola at Greater True Vine in Houston. My granddaughter played me your little recording.
That's Brother Wendell's count. He counts our choir in just that way every Sunday. Slow on the first two, like he's making sure the Lord is listening.
He don't know I'm calling. He'd tell me not to. So I'm calling.
It worked. It WORKED. Houston! Uncle Cross, how far is Houston?
Five hours, if the Choir don't boil over.
Tuesday cannot stop smiling. Ruth has not said a word. She has been watching Tuesday the whole time, the way you watch a pot.
Baby. Did you ask her?

afterLose.t: Second line don't end, baby, it just turns the corner. Come around again.
I have been marched wrong by the best. The tuba's waiting. Run it back.

afterChallenge.t: Watch Night, 1967. Twelve-twenty in the morning. Lantern Records was a brownstone two blocks from the church, with a party upstairs and a studio in the back room on the ground floor.
The back door stuck. The Professor knew to lift it and push. Snow came in with the five of them and melted on the linoleum.
Another Lantern act had been booked till one. Their singers had left at midnight for parties. A coffee cup was still warm on the console.
Twenty-two minutes of booked time were left on the clock above the glass. Somebody had paid for them. Nobody was using them.
Upstairs, a hundred people were celebrating a year that had already turned. You could hear them through the ceiling, clapping on one and three.
Gus Lark came down the back stairs in a dinner jacket with a paper plate in his hand. He had started out as an engineer. He still sat down at a board like it was his.
He looked at the five of them. He looked at the reel on the machine: most of it used, a little left at the end.
'Use the tail of the reel,' he said. He put the plate down on the console and pushed up his sleeves.
Dess, nineteen, stood by the door in her revue dress, holding her mother's tune in her mouth like a secret.
